facts.fact_text: On Sunday 2 February 2014, the applicant took part in a demonstration in Valladolid.
The demonstration on 2 February 2014 in Valladolid was against budgetary cuts and high unemployment rates, among other social issues.
The protest on 2 February 2014 in Valladolid was organised by an association in favour of unemployed people's rights called Asociación parad@s en movimiento Valladolid.
The protest of 2 February 2014 proceeded without incident until its official end.
After the official end of the demonstration on 2 February 2014, a group of around fifty to sixty protesters continued marching in the streets of Valladolid city centre.
The post-official-end protest on 2 February 2014 was spontaneous.
Immediately after the protesters stopped their march and stood in Plaza de San Lorenzo, the police approached them.
The police officers tried to remove the placard held by the protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The police officers held some of the protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo and pushed them away from the group in an attempt to dissolve the demonstration.
The police forced the protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo to put down the placard.
The protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo were forcefully separated by the police.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included pushing protesters to the ground.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included hitting protesters with truncheons.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included kicking protesters, even when they were already lying on the ground.
The applicant was holding the placard in the first line of the demonstration in Plaza de San Lorenzo when she was struck violently by a police officer.
The applicant suffered injuries to her mouth as a result of being struck by a police officer in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The applicant suffered injuries to her hand as a result of being struck by a police officer in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
Section 21(1) of the Spanish Constitution recognises the right to peaceful unarmed assembly and provides that the exercise of this right shall not require prior authorisation.

Section 21(2) of the Spanish Constitution provides that in the event of meetings in public places and of demonstrations, prior notification shall be given to the authorities, who may ban them only when there are well-founded grounds to expect a breach of public order, involving danger to persons or property.
Section 3(1) of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that meetings shall not be subject to prior authorisation.

Section 3(2) of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that the governmental authority shall protect meetings and demonstrations against those who attempt to prevent, disturb or undermine the lawful exercise of this right.

Section 5(a) of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that the government authority shall suspend and, if appropriate, dissolve meetings and demonstrations when they are considered unlawful under criminal law.

Section 5(b) of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that the government authority shall suspend and, if appropriate, dissolve meetings and demonstrations when disturbances of public order occur, endangering persons or property.

Section 5(c) of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that the government authority shall suspend and, if appropriate, dissolve meetings and demonstrations when paramilitary uniforms are worn by attendees.

Section 5 of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that resolutions to suspend or dissolve meetings and demonstrations shall be communicated beforehand to the attendees in the manner provided by law.

Section 8 of the Right of Assembly Act (Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983) provides that the holding of meetings in places of public transit and demonstrations must be communicated in writing to the corresponding governmental authority by their organisers or promoters.

Section 23(1) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that the relevant authorities shall adopt the necessary measures to protect the holding of assemblies and demonstrations, preventing the disruption of public safety.

Section 23(1) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that the authorities will order the dissolution of assemblies in places of public transit and of demonstrations in the cases established in section 5 of Institutional Law 9/1983 of 15 July 1983, regulating the right of assembly.

Section 23(1) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that the authorities will also disperse vehicles grouped together deliberately when these hamper, put in danger or hinder the traffic on those roads.

Section 23(2) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that intervention measures for the maintenance or reestablishment of public safety in assemblies and demonstrations shall be gradual and proportionate to the circumstances of the case.
Section 23(2) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that the dissolution of assemblies and demonstrations will constitute the last resort.

Section 23(3) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that before adopting dissolution measures, the acting units of the Security Forces and Corps shall warn the persons affected, even orally should the urgency of the situation make it unavoidable.

Section 23(3) of the Protection of Public Safety Act (Institutional Law 4/2015 of 30 March 2015) provides that in cases of public safety risk being posed by weapons, explosive devices or blunt objects, or any other objects dangerous in some way, the Security Forces and Corps shall be able to dissolve the assembly or demonstration or remove the vehicles and obstacles without the need for a prior warning.
On 2 February 2014, a political party was holding a congress in Valladolid.
On 2 February 2014, some politicians were having lunch in a restaurant located in Plaza de San Lorenzo when the group of protesters gathered in the square.
According to the police report, the protesters repeatedly tried to enter the restaurant in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
According to the police report, the protesters succeeded in interrupting the traffic in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo did not approach the entrance to the restaurant.
The protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo did not enter the restaurant's premises.
The protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo refused to put down the placard.
Some of the protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo tried to resist the police.
Tension escalated during the police intervention in Plaza de San Lorenzo on 2 February 2014.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included pushing protesters to the ground.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included hitting protesters with truncheons.
Some of the police officers' interventions in Plaza de San Lorenzo included kicking protesters, even when they were already lying on the ground.
One of the protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo tried unsuccessfully to take an officer's gun out of its holster.
The protester who tried to take an officer's gun out of its holster was subdued by the officer and arrested.
Two other protesters in Plaza de San Lorenzo were arrested for violent conduct or threats.
A fourth protester's arrest was ordered but the protester managed to escape from the police.
Two police officers were injured during the events in Plaza de San Lorenzo on 2 February 2014.
The applicant was holding the placard in the first line of the demonstration in Plaza de San Lorenzo when she was struck violently by a police officer.
The applicant suffered injuries to her mouth as a result of being struck by a police officer in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The applicant suffered injuries to her hand as a result of being struck by a police officer in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The applicant claimed that while protecting her head with her hand, her hand had been hit with a truncheon, which in turn had caused her to injure her mouth.
The applicant was taken to hospital for medical care following the events in Plaza de San Lorenzo on 2 February 2014.
According to the medical report, the applicant had suffered a direct trauma to her left hand.
According to the medical report, the applicant had an open cut in her head.
According to the medical report, the applicant had bruises in her head.
According to the medical report, the applicant had a fracture in her head.
According to the medical report, the applicant had inflammation in her head.
According to a medical report issued on 3 June 2014 by the Institute of Legal Medicine of Valladolid, the applicant's injuries had taken ninety days to heal.
According to the medical report issued on 3 June 2014 by the Institute of Legal Medicine of Valladolid, during the ninety days of healing the applicant was not able to perform her usual activities.
Another medical report, issued after 3 June 2014, stated that the applicant's injuries had completely impeded her return to her usual activities.
On 15 February 2016, the applicant was given the status of 'permanently incapacitated to perform her usual activities' as a consequence of her injuries suffered on 2 February 2014.

According to the police report, the protesters succeeded in interrupting the traffic in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
The police report noted that the applicant had been among the six protesters who had had to be taken to hospital for treatment of injuries.

The Audiencia Provincial of Valladolid stated that the police intervention had been justified not because the protesters had tried to enter the restaurant, for which there was no evidence, but because the protesters had been holding a placard with which they had occupied a public road, preventing the movement of vehicles and people.

The Audiencia Provincial of Valladolid stated that everything had been due to a police response to a situation of violence and disorder generated by people who had refused to abide by police orders to dissolve the demonstration and remove the placard.

The Audiencia Provincial of Valladolid stated that the individuals had refused to identify themselves properly, kicked, struggled, insulted and pushed the police officers, who had had to repel that action, resulting in injuries on both sides.

The Audiencia Provincial of Valladolid stated that what differentiated one action from another was that the police had acted legitimately, while the demonstrators had opposed the actions of the police in an active and violent manner.
The judgment of 20 April 2018 by Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 stated that it could be seen in the footage that police officers were kicking people.
Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 found that the attitude and behaviour of the protesters had not justified the indiscriminate use of force by the police against them.
Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 found that the protesters had not impeded the movement of traffic.
Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 found that the protesters had not threatened anyone.
Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 found that the protesters had not tried to enter the restaurant in Plaza de San Lorenzo.
Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 found that the protesters had not attacked the police officers.

Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 stated that the right to freedom of assembly had been violated when the only response after the end of the official demonstration had been to use force even when there had been no danger to the physical integrity of the people inside the restaurant.
In the view of Valladolid criminal judge no. 3, the protest had been violently dispersed without any prior warning to dissolve the demonstration or to put down the placard.
In a judgment of 27 March 2019, the Audiencia Nacional found that the State was liable for the conduct of the police agents who had intervened in the dispersal of the protest on 2 February 2014.
In its judgment of 27 March 2019, the Audiencia Nacional found that the police intervention on 2 February 2014 had been disproportionate in its response to the group of protesters.
In its judgment of 27 March 2019, the Audiencia Nacional found that the police intervention on 2 February 2014 had been disproportionate in view of the force used against the applicant.
In its judgment of 27 March 2019, the Audiencia Nacional found that the applicant had no legal duty to bear the damage caused to her purely because she had taken part in the protest.
Among the evidence considered by the Audiencia Nacional in its judgment of 27 March 2019 were videos provided and the statements of two witnesses.
The Audiencia Nacional took into account the judgment of 20 April 2018 given by Valladolid criminal judge no. 3 and reproduced that text in full in its judgment of 27 March 2019.
The Audiencia Nacional ordered the Spanish administration to pay the applicant 10,000 euros in its judgment of 27 March 2019.

The amount of 10,000 euros was fixed by the Audiencia Nacional taking into account the standard harmonised amounts for redress established as guidelines for cases such as the present one in domestic legislation.

The amount of 10,000 euros was fixed by the Audiencia Nacional taking into account the seriousness of the applicant's injuries, the number of days needed to heal, the damage to her appearance and the sequelae.
